entries.meaning: A building that people live in, usually one family per building. ---
examples: They bought a house on the north side of town.
All the houses on this street were built in the fifties.
Come over to my house after work.
entries.contrast: The plural houses is pronounced HOW-ziz — the s turns into a z sound.

entries.meaning: The place where someone lives and feels they belong. ---
examples: I work from home three days a week.
They're saving up for their first home.
It took him two hours to get home in the snow.
entries.contrast: A house is the building; a home is where you live. And you go home, never "to home".

entries.meaning: A structure with a roof and walls, such as a house or office block. ---
examples: Our office is in the tall building across from the park.
Half the buildings downtown are empty now.
You need a keycard to get into the building after six.

entries.meaning: A set of rooms for living in, on one floor of a larger building. ---
examples: She rents a one-bedroom apartment near campus.
The apartments on the top floor have a view of the river.
We're moving into a bigger apartment in June.
entries.contrast: Americans say apartment; the British say flat.

entries.meaning: A room used for sleeping in. ---
examples: The house has three bedrooms and one bath.
Keep your voice down — the baby's asleep in the bedroom.
My bedroom is the one at the end of the hall.

entries.meaning: A room with a toilet and usually a sink and a bath or shower. ---
examples: Excuse me, where's the bathroom?
Both bathrooms need new tile.
He's been in the bathroom for twenty minutes.
entries.contrast: In American English the bathroom normally contains the toilet, so asking for the bathroom in a restaurant means the toilet.

entries.meaning: The main room in a home where people sit, talk and relax. ---
examples: We watched the game in the living room.
The living room gets great light in the afternoon.
Most of these apartments have tiny living rooms.

entries.meaning: A room where meals are eaten at a table. ---
examples: We only use the dining room on holidays.
She set the table in the dining room for eight.
Older houses around here all have formal dining rooms.

entries.meaning: The floor of a building that is below ground level. ---
examples: The washer and dryer are down in the basement.
Our basement floods every spring.
A lot of basements in this neighborhood have been turned into apartments.

entries.meaning: The space directly under the roof of a house, often used for storage. ---
examples: The Christmas decorations are up in the attic.
We found my grandmother's letters in the attic.
There's a squirrel living in the attic again.

entries.meaning: A building or part of a house where a car is kept. ---
examples: Park in the garage — it's supposed to hail.
His band practices in the garage.
The house has a two-car garage.
entries.contrast: Americans stress the second syllable, guh-RAHZH; the British say GA-rij.

entries.meaning: A long narrow passage inside a building with rooms opening off it. ---
examples: Leave your boots in the hallway.
The bedrooms are down that hallway on the left.
The hallways in this building are always freezing.

entries.meaning: A small storage room built into the wall of a house. ---
examples: Your coat's in the hall closet.
This bedroom doesn't have a closet.
I cleaned out both closets over the weekend.
entries.contrast: An American closet is built into the wall, not a free-standing piece of furniture.

entries.meaning: A covered platform at the entrance to a house. ---
examples: They sat out on the porch until it got dark.
The package is on the front porch.
A lot of the old houses here have wraparound porches.

entries.meaning: A platform with a railing that sticks out from an upper wall of a building. ---
examples: Our room had a small balcony facing the ocean.
She keeps herbs out on the balcony.
The apartments with balconies cost more.

entries.meaning: A flat wooden platform built outside a house for sitting on. ---
examples: We're grilling out on the deck.
The deck needs to be resealed this summer.
He built the deck himself over two weekends.

entries.meaning: The area of ground around a house, usually with grass. ---
examples: The kids are playing in the back yard.
We have a huge yard and nobody to mow it.
Most of the yards on this block have fences.
entries.contrast: The grass around an American house is the yard; the British would call it the garden.

entries.meaning: A piece of ground where flowers or vegetables are grown. ---
examples: She grows tomatoes in the garden every year.
The garden is completely overgrown.
The botanical gardens are free on Tuesdays.

entries.meaning: A short private road leading from the street to a house or garage. ---
examples: There's a strange car in our driveway.
He shoveled the driveway before breakfast.
Both driveways were blocked by the delivery truck.

entries.meaning: The open area just inside the main entrance of a large building. ---
examples: Wait for me in the lobby.
The hotel lobby smelled like chlorine.
They redid the lobbies in both towers.

entries.meaning: A long passage in a building with doors along it. ---
examples: His office is at the end of the corridor.
We got lost in the corridors of the hospital.
The corridor was lined with framed photographs.

entries.meaning: A room in a home set up for a baby or small child. ---
examples: They painted the nursery pale green.
The monitor picks up every sound from the nursery.
Both nurseries were done before the twins arrived.

entries.meaning: An open upper space under a roof, or an apartment made from an old factory floor. ---
examples: He rents a loft in a converted warehouse.
The hay is stored up in the loft.
The lofts downtown all have exposed brick.

entries.meaning: A small comfortable room in a house used for reading, watching TV or working. ---
examples: Dad's asleep in the den again.
We turned the spare bedroom into a den.
The listing says three bedrooms plus a den.

entries.meaning: A room with toilets in a public building. ---
examples: The restroom is past the elevators on your right.
Both restrooms were out of paper towels.
Is there a restroom I can use?

entries.meaning: A room where someone works at a desk. ---
examples: She works out of a home office upstairs.
Come by my office around three.
All the corner offices have windows on two sides.

entries.meaning: The small entrance area just inside the front door of a house or theater. ---
examples: Leave the umbrella in the foyer.
The foyer has a chandelier and a marble floor.
People were still milling around the foyer at intermission.

entries.meaning: A set of connected rooms, especially in a hotel. ---
examples: They put us in a suite on the top floor.
The office suite takes up half the eighth floor.
All the suites come with a small kitchen.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like sweet — not like suit.

entries.meaning: A vertical structure that encloses a room or building. ---
examples: Hang the mirror on that wall.
The walls are so thin you can hear everything.
We knocked out a wall to open up the kitchen.

entries.meaning: The upper inside surface of a room. ---
examples: There's a water stain on the ceiling.
The apartment has ten-foot ceilings.
He painted the ceiling and got more on himself than on it.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like sealing.

entries.meaning: The flat surface you walk on inside a building, or one level of a building. ---
examples: Don't leave your bag on the floor.
We're on the fourth floor.
The kitchen floor is real oak under that linoleum.

entries.meaning: A flat panel that opens and closes an entrance to a room or building. ---
examples: Shut the door — you're letting the heat out.
Someone's at the door.
All the interior doors stick in humid weather.

entries.meaning: An opening in a wall filled with glass that lets in light. ---
examples: Open a window — it's stuffy in here.
The windows rattle whenever a truck goes by.
She sat by the window and watched it rain.

entries.meaning: The opening in a wall that a door fits into. ---
examples: He stood in the doorway with his coat still on.
The couch won't fit through that doorway.
They widened both doorways for the wheelchair.

entries.meaning: The round handle you turn to open a door. ---
examples: The doorknob came off in my hand.
She hung the bag on the doorknob so she wouldn't forget it.
We replaced all the doorknobs with brass ones.
entries.contrast: The k in -knob is silent: DOR-nahb.

entries.meaning: The part of a door, drawer or bag that you hold to open or carry it. ---
examples: Pull the handle toward you, don't push.
The handle on the freezer is loose.
All the cabinet handles are the same brushed nickel.

entries.meaning: The metal joint that a door or lid swings on. ---
examples: That hinge needs oil — listen to it squeak.
The gate came off its hinges in the storm.
He unscrewed the hinges to get the door off.

entries.meaning: A device on a door that keeps it shut until it is opened with a key or code. ---
examples: The lock on the back door is broken.
We changed the locks after we moved in.
He jiggled the key in the lock until it turned.

entries.meaning: The strip of floor at the bottom of a doorway. ---
examples: He carried her over the threshold.
The wood at the threshold is worn smooth.
New thresholds went in with the flooring.

entries.meaning: The step just outside an outer door. ---
examples: The newspaper was still on the doorstep at noon.
She left the flowers on his doorstep and drove off.
Salt the doorsteps before it ices over.

entries.meaning: One of the flat surfaces you put your foot on when going up or down. ---
examples: Watch that bottom step — it's loose.
The kids were sitting on the front steps.
There's one more step than you think at the top.

entries.meaning: A set of stairs inside a building, together with its supports and rail. ---
examples: A wide staircase curved up from the entryway.
The back staircase leads straight to the kitchen.
Both staircases are original to the house.

entries.meaning: The rail along the side of a staircase that you hold on to. ---
examples: Hold the banister on the way down.
He used to slide down the banister as a kid.
The banister was refinished last year.

entries.meaning: A bar or fence along the edge of stairs, a balcony or a porch. ---
examples: Don't lean on that railing — it's rotted.
The railing on the deck needs replacing.
They painted all the iron railings black.

entries.meaning: A machine that carries people up and down between floors of a building. ---
examples: Take the elevator to the ninth floor.
Both elevators are out again.
We got stuck in the elevator for half an hour.
entries.contrast: American elevator = British lift.

entries.meaning: The flat area at the top of a flight of stairs or between two flights. ---
examples: There's a window on the landing.
He stopped on the landing to catch his breath.
The landings are wide enough for a chair.

entries.meaning: A vertical pipe or structure that carries smoke up out of a building. ---
examples: You should get the chimney swept before winter.
Birds built a nest in the chimney.
The old brick chimneys are what give the street its character.

entries.meaning: An opening in a wall where a fire is built. ---
examples: We hung the stockings over the fireplace.
The fireplace hasn't worked in years.
Two of the bedrooms have their own fireplaces.

entries.meaning: The floor of a fireplace and the stone area in front of it. ---
examples: The cat sleeps on the hearth all winter.
He set the kindling down on the stone hearth.
The old hearths were built of fieldstone.
entries.contrast: Spelled like heart plus h, but the vowel is the one in car, not the one in earth.

entries.meaning: The shelf above a fireplace. ---
examples: Their wedding photo sits on the mantel.
She dusted the mantel and put the candles back.
The mantels in both rooms are solid walnut.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like mantle.

entries.meaning: A channel along the edge of a roof that carries rainwater away. ---
examples: The gutter is full of leaves again.
He fell off the ladder cleaning the gutters.
Water was pouring straight over the gutter.

entries.meaning: A long thick piece of wood or metal that supports part of a building. ---
examples: That wall can't come out — there's a beam behind it.
The ceiling has exposed wooden beams.
A steel beam runs the length of the basement.

entries.meaning: A tall upright post that supports part of a building. ---
examples: The courthouse has six white columns out front.
A concrete column holds up the parking deck.
They wrapped the porch columns in new trim.
entries.contrast: The final n is silent: KAH-luhm.

entries.meaning: A curved structure over an opening such as a door or window. ---
examples: There's a stone arch over the front gate.
The hallway ends in a low arch.
The arches along the courtyard are original.

entries.meaning: A rounded roof shaped like half a ball. ---
examples: You can see the capitol dome from the highway.
Light comes in through the glass dome overhead.
The domes were covered in copper that's gone green.

entries.meaning: The solid base built underground that a building rests on. ---
examples: There's a crack in the foundation.
They poured the foundation last week.
Older houses on this street have stone foundations.

entries.meaning: The front outside face of a building. ---
examples: They kept the original facade and gutted everything behind it.
The glass facade reflects the whole square.
Several facades on the block are landmarked.
entries.contrast: The c is pronounced like s — fuh-SAHD, from French façade.

entries.meaning: The door or gate by which you go into a place. ---
examples: Use the side entrance after nine.
We'll meet you at the main entrance.
The building has entrances on two streets.
entries.contrast: The noun is EN-truhns; the unrelated verb entrance (to enchant) is en-TRANS.

entries.meaning: A door or opening for going out of a building. ---
examples: The emergency exit is at the back of the theater.
Please note the nearest exit.
All the exits were blocked with boxes.

entries.meaning: A passage between rows of seats or shelves. ---
examples: Ketchup is in aisle six.
She walked down the aisle to organ music.
The aisles in that store are too narrow for a cart.
entries.contrast: The s is silent — it sounds exactly like I'll.

entries.meaning: The place where two walls or edges meet. ---
examples: Put the lamp in that corner.
There's a spiderweb in the corner of the ceiling.
All four corners of the room are crooked.

entries.meaning: The narrow board running along the bottom of an interior wall. ---
examples: The baseboard is scuffed up behind the couch.
We painted the baseboards white.
There's a gap between the baseboard and the floor.
entries.contrast: American baseboard = British skirting board.

entries.meaning: A hinged wooden or metal cover on the outside of a window. ---
examples: One shutter is hanging crooked.
They closed the shutters before the storm hit.
The blue shutters really make the house stand out.

entries.meaning: A window cover made of slats or a roll of material that pulls down. ---
examples: Can you close the blinds? The sun's in my eyes.
One slat on the blind is bent.
We put up wooden blinds in the bedroom.

entries.meaning: A piece of cloth hung across a window or opening. ---
examples: Pull the curtains — the neighbors can see in.
The shower curtain is coming off its rings.
She sewed the curtains herself.

entries.meaning: The narrow ledge along the bottom of a window. ---
examples: She keeps a row of basil on the kitchen windowsill.
The cat sleeps on the windowsill all afternoon.
Paint was peeling off both windowsills.

entries.meaning: A single sheet of glass in a window or door. ---
examples: A pane cracked when the ball hit it.
The old windows have six panes each.
He replaced the broken pane himself.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like pain.

entries.meaning: The border or structure that holds a door, window or picture in place. ---
examples: The door frame is warped, so it won't latch.
Water got in around the window frame.
All the frames are aluminum, not wood.

entries.meaning: A fine mesh in a window or door that keeps insects out. ---
examples: There's a hole in the screen and the flies are getting in.
We take the screens out every fall.
The porch has screens on three sides.

entries.meaning: The hole in a lock that a key goes into. ---
examples: He couldn't find the keyhole in the dark.
Light was coming through the keyhole.
The keyholes on these antique doors are enormous.

entries.meaning: A button by a door that rings a bell inside. ---
examples: The doorbell rang right as we sat down to eat.
Their doorbell has a camera in it now.
Half the doorbells in the building don't work.

entries.meaning: A speaker system for talking between the entrance and the apartments inside. ---
examples: Buzz me in — I'll ring the intercom.
The intercom crackles so badly you can't hear anything.
New intercoms went in when they renovated the lobby.

entries.meaning: A hard block of baked clay used for building walls. ---
examples: The house is brick on three sides and siding on the fourth.
A few bricks have come loose near the chimney.
He propped the door open with a brick.
entries.countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance

entries.meaning: A hard building material made from cement, sand, gravel and water. ---
examples: They poured the concrete for the patio yesterday.
The floor is bare concrete.
Frost got under the concrete and cracked it.
entries.contrast: As a noun Americans stress the first syllable: KAHN-kreet.

entries.meaning: A soft paste spread on walls and ceilings that dries hard and smooth. ---
examples: Plaster was falling off the ceiling in chunks.
The walls are old plaster, not drywall.
He patched the hole with plaster and sanded it flat.
entries.contrast: In Britain a plaster is also a small sticking bandage; Americans call that a Band-Aid.

entries.meaning: Flat panels of gypsum board used to make interior walls. ---
examples: We hung drywall in the basement over the weekend.
The movers put a hole right through the drywall.
There's just drywall between the two units.
entries.contrast: American drywall = British plasterboard.

entries.meaning: A thin flat piece of baked clay or stone used to cover floors, walls or roofs. ---
examples: The bathroom floor is tile.
Two tiles cracked when he dropped the wrench.
They're putting subway tile behind the stove.
entries.countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance

entries.meaning: Thick woven material that covers a floor. ---
examples: There's wall-to-wall carpet in every bedroom.
We pulled up the carpet and found hardwood underneath.
The carpets in the hallway are worn through.
entries.countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance

entries.meaning: Decorated paper glued to the walls of a room. ---
examples: The wallpaper is peeling in the corner.
We steamed off three layers of old wallpaper.
She picked out wallpaper with little blue flowers.
entries.contrast: Uncountable in English, though «обои» is plural in Russian: the wallpaper is peeling, never "wallpapers are".

entries.meaning: Material put in walls and roofs to keep heat in or out. ---
examples: There's almost no insulation in the attic.
Blowing in insulation cut our heating bill in half.
The old insulation had gotten damp and moldy.

entries.meaning: Colored liquid spread on a surface to protect or decorate it. ---
examples: The paint in the hallway is chipping.
We need one more gallon of paint to finish the trim.
Exterior paints have to hold up to sun and rain.
entries.countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance

entries.meaning: A temporary framework of poles and planks that workers stand on. ---
examples: There's scaffolding across the whole front of the building.
They finally took down the scaffolding after two years.
Workers were putting up scaffolding at six in the morning.
entries.contrast: Uncountable in English even though «леса» is plural in Russian: some scaffolding, not "a scaffolding".

entries.meaning: A long container you fill with water and sit in to wash. ---
examples: The bathtub drains really slowly.
She was reading in the bathtub until the water went cold.
Both bathtubs are the old cast-iron kind.

entries.meaning: A fixture that sprays water over you for washing, or the act of washing there. ---
examples: The shower takes forever to get hot.
I'm going to jump in the shower real quick.
The new bathroom has a walk-in shower.

entries.meaning: The bowl-shaped fixture used for getting rid of body waste. ---
examples: The toilet keeps running after you flush.
He fixed the toilet with a five-dollar part.
All the toilets on that floor were out of order.
entries.contrast: In American English toilet means the fixture itself; the room is the bathroom or restroom.

entries.meaning: The hole and pipe that carries used water away. ---
examples: Something's stuck in the shower drain.
Don't pour grease down the drain.
All the drains in the basement back up when it rains hard.

entries.meaning: An opening that lets air move into or out of a room. ---
examples: Cold air is blowing straight out of that vent.
The dryer vent is clogged with lint.
Close the vents in the rooms you're not using.

entries.meaning: A tube that carries water, gas or waste through a building. ---
examples: A pipe burst under the sink.
The pipes rattle whenever someone runs the shower.
Wrap the outside pipes before the first freeze.

entries.meaning: The system of pipes and fixtures that carries water through a building. ---
examples: The plumbing in this place is a hundred years old.
They had to redo all the plumbing before we moved in.
Something's wrong with the plumbing upstairs.
entries.contrast: The b is silent: PLUHM-ing.

entries.meaning: The system of electrical wires inside a building. ---
examples: The wiring in the older part of the house isn't up to code.
An electrician checked the wiring before closing.
Faulty wiring is what started the fire.

entries.meaning: The place in a wall where you plug in an electrical device. ---
examples: Is there an outlet behind the couch?
This room only has two outlets.
The outlet by the sink stopped working.
entries.contrast: American outlet = British socket or power point.

entries.meaning: The small device on a wall that turns a light on and off. ---
examples: The switch is on your left as you come in.
One of these switches controls the porch light.
He flipped the switch and nothing happened.

entries.meaning: A metal heating unit that warms a room with hot water or steam. ---
examples: The radiator clanks all night long.
Don't put the couch right against the radiator.
Half the radiators in the building are cold.

entries.meaning: The machine that heats a whole house, usually in the basement. ---
examples: The furnace quit on the coldest night of the year.
We had the furnace serviced in October.
New furnaces are a lot more efficient.

entries.meaning: A device on a wall that controls the heating or cooling. ---
examples: Somebody turned the thermostat down to sixty.
We put in a smart thermostat last year.
The thermostats on each floor are set separately.

entries.meaning: A door in a fence or wall around a yard or property. ---
examples: Latch the gate so the dog doesn't get out.
The gate squeaks every time it swings.
Both gates are padlocked at night.
entries.contrast: One gate is a gate — countable and singular — even though «ворота» is plural in Russian.

entries.meaning: A barrier of wood, wire or metal around a piece of land. ---
examples: The fence between us and the neighbors is falling down.
They put up a six-foot fence around the pool.
All the fences on that side blew over.

entries.meaning: A narrow way for walking, made by use or laid with stone. ---
examples: A stone path runs from the driveway to the door.
Stay on the path — the grass is wet.
The paths through the park are lit until midnight.
entries.contrast: Americans say /pæθ/ with the vowel of cat; the plural paths ends in a voiced sound, PATHZ.

entries.meaning: A flat paved outdoor area next to a building. ---
examples: They serve lunch on the terrace in good weather.
The terrace looks out over the whole valley.
The upper terraces are for residents only.

entries.meaning: A small simple building used for storing tools or equipment. ---
examples: The lawnmower's in the shed out back.
He built the shed from a kit.
Both sheds need a coat of paint.

entries.meaning: A large farm building for animals, crops or machinery. ---
examples: The horses are already in the barn.
They converted the old barn into a wedding venue.
You can see red barns all along that highway.

entries.meaning: A glass building where plants are grown in warm conditions. ---
examples: She starts her seedlings in the greenhouse in February.
It's about ninety degrees in that greenhouse.
The nursery has four greenhouses out back.

entries.meaning: An area of short cut grass around a house or building. ---
examples: I have to mow the lawn before it rains.
Their lawn is greener than anyone else's on the street.
The lawns all went brown in the drought.

entries.meaning: A row of bushes planted close together as a boundary. ---
examples: The hedge along the driveway needs trimming.
A tall hedge blocks the view from the road.
He spent all Saturday cutting the hedges.

entries.meaning: A box outside a house or in a lobby where letters are delivered. ---
examples: Can you check the mailbox on your way in?
Someone knocked over our mailbox with a truck.
The mailboxes are just inside the front door.
entries.contrast: American mailbox = British letterbox or postbox.

entries.meaning: A small simple house, usually in the country or by a lake. ---
examples: They rent a cottage on the lake every August.
The cottage has one bedroom and a woodstove.
There are half a dozen cottages along the shore.

entries.meaning: A small house made of wood, usually in the woods or mountains. ---
examples: We spent the weekend at his cabin in the mountains.
The cabin has no running water.
The camp has twelve cabins along the creek.

entries.meaning: A very large and impressive house. ---
examples: The governor lives in a mansion downtown.
That whole street is nothing but mansions.
The mansion was turned into a museum in the sixties.

entries.meaning: An apartment that the resident owns rather than rents. ---
examples: They sold the house and bought a condo near the beach.
The condo board voted to fix the roof.
Condos in that building start at four hundred thousand.

entries.meaning: A very tall building with many floors. ---
examples: You can see the skyscrapers from thirty miles out.
They're putting up another skyscraper on the waterfront.
The skyscraper sways a little in high wind.

entries.meaning: One level of a building. ---
examples: It's a two-story house with a finished basement.
The parking garage is six stories tall.
He fell one story and walked away without a scratch.
entries.contrast: Americans spell the level of a building story; the British write storey.

entries.meaning: A piece of furniture or recess with a door, used for storing dishes or food. ---
examples: The glasses are in the cupboard over the sink.
She went through every cupboard looking for the cinnamon.
The cupboard doors don't shut all the way.
entries.contrast: The p is silent and the vowel is short: KUHB-urd, not "cup-board".

entries.meaning: A flat work surface in a kitchen, or a long table you are served at. ---
examples: Just set the groceries on the counter.
We wiped down all the counters after dinner.
He ate at the counter instead of taking a booth.

entries.meaning: The art and style of designing buildings. ---
examples: She studied architecture for two years and switched to design.
The architecture downtown is mostly nineteenth century.
I love the architecture in that part of the city.

entries.meaning: The work of building things such as houses and roads. ---
examples: The new wing is still under construction.
He's worked in construction since high school.
Construction on the bridge starts in the spring.

entries.meaning: The work of repairing and improving an old building.
examples: The kitchen renovation took four months instead of six weeks.
The library is closed for renovations.
They financed the renovation with a home equity loan.
entries.contrast: Russian «ремонт» of a home is a renovation or remodel — "repair" means fixing something broken.
